Welcome!

My name is Nick Wilson,{{< marginnote >}}Formally, I am an Associate Professor of Sociology at Stony Brook University, but I don’t particularly like such trappings, especially in person, so please just call me “Nick.” Note, however, that many of your professors will want to be addressed formally![ ] and these are my extended lecture notes to Introduction to Sociology. I’ve been teaching this course here at Stony Brook University since the Fall of 2016.

Why these notes?

Over the course of teaching introduction to sociology (with enrollments of around 250 students), I’ve grown increasingly dissatisfied with the textbook I was using, and, indeed, any one that I could find. This was for several reasons.

  1. Cost. Most textbooks seem unjustifiably expensive today. A quick glance at Amazon shows that they can range from $30 to over $150 to buy, and still a substantial amount of money to rent.
  2. Quality. While most textbooks are nominally written by well-known academics, as we will see, sociology is a notoriously difficult subject to even introduce, so the quality of textbooks varies wildly, both within and among the different offerings.
  3. Voice. {{< marginnote >}}I think I am most influenced by the writing styles of George Orwell (in “Politics and the English Language”), Christopher Lasch (in Plain Style), and Strunk and White’s Elements of Style.{{< /marginnote >}}You will find that I prefer to write prose in a direct, conversational, active style, and this is something that is surprisingly hard to find in a textbook. Even ones that are written “simply” tend to overdo the passive voice, pointlessly elevate jargon, exaggerate the unity and certainty of sociology’s findings, and employ other false trappings of scientific authority.
  4. Datedness. {{< marginnote >}}For instance, it is only now that textbooks are even acknowledging, much less considering the impact of, COVID-19.{{< /marginnote >}} Because traditional textbooks take so long to conceive, write, vet, and physically produce, they are usually surprisingly dated by the time they are published.
  5. Intellectual divergence. Finally, I also noticed that I increasingly disagreed with most available textbooks. I especially chafed at them oversimplifying sociology. In my view, the field is ambiguous, difficult, and challenging; indeed, it is one of the hardest sciences to practice, because it has the most complex object of study–society itself. By extension, I have come to believe that an introduction to sociology should be clear, but not simple.

With those reasons in mind, beginning in the summer of 2024 I decided to transform and extend my lecture slides into these notes, and I worked intensively to complete the first draft of these notes in the first half of 2026.

Structure of these notes

These notes consist of twenty chapters and an introduction. To begin, discuss how to use these notes, and how their style reflects how I think about sociology (and how I believe you should too!)

Part I

Then, in Part I, I discuss sociology’s distintive intellectual style and heritage,{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 1: Imagination.{{< /sidenote >}} its place among other disciplines,{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 2: Discipline.{{< /sidenote >}} and then its (several) methods and their benefits and challenges of each.{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 3: Methods.{{< /sidenote >}}

Part II

After that, since this a course meant to introduce you to the field, the bulk of the notes, comprising six chapters, is in Part II, which oulines what I consider to be the fundamental conceptual building blocks in sociology. I think sociology is fundamentally oriented around the intersection of meaning and action,{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 4: Meaning and Action.{{< /sidenote >}} especially in contexts of interaction,{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 5: Interaction.{{< /sidenote >}} is usually organized following social structures,{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 6: Social Structure.{{< /sidenote >}} the result of which are qualities we have usually called identities or selves.{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 7: Identity.{{< /sidenote >}} Finally, there are two special characteristics of social structures that are such common features of sociological analysis that they have become foundational: that your place in social structures is not what it is only because of everyone’s agreement, but also because of power and discipline;{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 8: Power and Discipline.{{< /sidenote >}} and that, especially in complex societies, almost every social structure exhibits some form of inequality.{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 9: Inequality.{{< /sidenote >}}

Part III

Part III combines these building blocks, along with the two world-historical shifts of central interest to sociologists (the emergence and eventual dominance of capitalism and the rise, transformation, and dissolution of large empires) to understand key features of the era in which we live, “modernity.” The forces at work in this era are different from what came before in critical ways, and affect everything from our identites–our sense of race and ethnicity {{< sidenote >}}Chapter 10: Race and Ethnicity.{{< /sidenote >}}, gender and sexuality {{< sidenote >}}Chapter 11: Gender and Sexuality.{{< /sidenote >}}, and even how we imagine our place in the world{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 12: Globalization.{{< /sidenote >}}–and has decisively reorganized our lives through political{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 13: Politics.{{< /sidenote >}}, economic{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 14: Economics.{{< /sidenote >}}, intellectual{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 15: Education.{{< /sidenote >}}, and even biological{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 16: Health.{{< /sidenote >}} change.

Part IV

One key cultural feature of modernity is that it does not define any particular end for our global society. Instead, sociologists have recognized that it tends to express four tensions, which are the subject of Part IV. The first tension is that, while people are collectively organized to a level we have never before seen in human history, we struggle to feel our social obligations to one another, and are at risk to regress into polarized camps, which in turn can lead to decay and even violence.{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 17: Polarization.{{< /sidenote >}} Second, while a distinctive human skill, the employment of technology on a large scale, has led to unimaginable abundance and ease, it also risks slipping beyond our collective control.{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 18: Technology.{{< /sidenote >}} Third, one of the key domains this technological dynamic has played out is in our relationship to the environment, and especially anthropogenic climate change.{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 19:The Environment.{{< /sidenote >}} Finally, the notes close by reflecting on the search for meaning in the modern world, and what it takes to live a long, happy, fulfilling life.{{< sidenote >}}Chapter 20: Flourishing.{{< /sidenote >}}
